quiz.question: 1. Why should you record the xv6 source commit before making changes?
options: A. To guarantee the code has no bugs
B. To identify the exact revision used and reproduce the build
C. To make QEMU run faster
D. To avoid writing tests
quiz.explanation: Recording the exact commit hash via 'git rev-parse HEAD' ensures that your work, build scripts, and test findings are fully reproducible by other engineers and evaluators against the identical codebase.

quiz.question: 2. What connects a user-space syscall wrapper to its kernel implementation?
options: A. Only the Makefile
B. The syscall number, trap path, dispatch table, and handler integration
C. The filesystem alone
D. A hardware timer only
quiz.explanation: A system call requires end-to-end wiring: the user wrapper triggers ecall with a syscall number in a7, the trap handler preserves user state, syscall() dispatches via a function pointer table, and the kernel handler stores the return value in a0.

quiz.question: 3. Why must a process's parent pointer be accessed according to the kernel's synchronization rules?
options: A. Because all pointers are invalid in kernel code
B. Because process exit and reparenting can change lifecycle relationships
C. Because QEMU prevents concurrent execution
D. Because parent pointers are always user memory
quiz.explanation: In a concurrent kernel, a parent process might terminate and call exit(), reparenting child processes to init (PID 1) while a concurrent thread is reading the pointer. Reading without holding the proper lock causes a dangerous use-after-free or torn pointer race.

quiz.question: 4. What should you do if xv6 fails before your extension is implemented?
options: A. Ignore the failure and continue
B. Change unrelated kernel code immediately
C. Investigate and establish a working baseline before attributing failures to your change
D. Report the failure as proof the extension is incorrect
quiz.explanation: Always verify that the clean, unmodified repository builds, boots in QEMU, and passes existing tests before adding changes. Otherwise, environment or toolchain flaws will be mistaken for kernel bugs.

quiz.question: 5. What is the purpose of the final technical report?
options: A. To claim production readiness
B. To demonstrate implementation, tests, evidence, limitations, and reproducibility
C. To replace source code
D. To report only successful tests
quiz.explanation: Engineering reports provide verifiable evidence: requirements, architecture diagrams, test matrices with actual outputs, failure investigations, and explicit documentation of assumptions and limitations.

theorySections.title: Modifying, Extending, and Validating a Real RISC-V Operating System
paragraphs: This capstone is the practical culmination of your operating systems journey. You will set up an emulator environment, trace boot and trap transitions on bare-metal RISC-V, implement a thread-safe system call extension (`getppid`), instrument kernel memory or scheduling, and deliver a formal 12-section systems engineering report.

theorySections.title: Setting Up a Reproducible xv6/RISC-V Environment

theorySections.title: Understanding the Boot Sequence and Source Tree Topology
paragraphs: Explore how bare-metal hardware bootstraps into machine mode (M-Mode), delegates interrupts to supervisor mode (S-Mode), initializes subsystems, and spawns the first user-space process.
Step through the 5 phases of kernel boot from hardware reset to user shell.
{bootStages[bootStage].desc}
Process table management, process allocation (`allocproc`), state transitions, and round-robin scheduler.
User and kernel trap handlers (`usertrap`, `kerneltrap`), interrupt vectoring, and syscall dispatch trigger.
System call dispatch table (`syscalls[]`), argument retrieval helpers (`argint`, `argaddr`, `argstr`).
Process-related syscall implementations (`sys_fork`, `sys_exit`, `sys_wait`, `sys_getpid`).

theorySections.title: Tracing Execution Across the User / Kernel Boundary
paragraphs: A system call transitions execution from unprivileged User mode (U-mode) into privileged Supervisor mode (S-mode) via the RISC-V `ecall` hardware instruction.
Step through the exact user-to-kernel boundary transitions for getppid().

theorySections.title: Designing and Implementing the getppid() System Call
paragraphs: Add a bounded, thread-safe system call that returns the parent process ID (`getppid()`). Follow the 7-file integration workflow used by professional systems engineers.
Compare an unsynchronized dereference with a lock-guarded parent read.

theorySections.title: Automated Kernel Testing and Grade Suite Validation
paragraphs: Kernel extensions must be validated with dedicated user-space test suites covering parent invocations, child fork verification, multiple concurrent children, and reparenting lifecycle behavior.
Run simulated make grade to test getppid() against the complete test matrix.

theorySections.title: Instrumenting Process Scheduling or Memory Behavior
paragraphs: A kernel extension must not only return correct values—it must allow engineers to observe how the operating system behaves under execution.
Instrument `scheduler()` in kernel/proc.c: record when a process transitions from RUNNABLE to RUNNING and when its CPU time slice yields.
Instrument physical page allocation in kernel/kalloc.c: trace page allocations, free list consumption, and out-of-memory handling.
Instrument kernel/syscall.c: log syscall numbers and return values, measuring execution latency across user/kernel switches.

Do not insert unconditional printf statements in high-frequency loops (such as the scheduler)! UART serial printing is synchronous and slow; console flooding alters thread scheduling timing and masks concurrency races.
